clinicalPearls: A delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction in which ultraviolet light (usually UVA) converts a topically applied or, less often, systemic chemical into an allergen the immune system then reacts to
Presents as an eczematous, sometimes vesicular, itchy eruption favouring sun-exposed sites such as the face, V of the neck, dorsa of the hands and forearms
Characteristically spares shaded areas including the upper eyelids, submental region, behind the ears and beneath the chin, which helps distinguish it from an airborne dermatitis
Common culprits include organic ultraviolet filters in sunscreens, topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g. ketoprofen), fragrances and certain antimicrobials
Unlike phototoxicity, it requires prior sensitisation, affects only a minority of exposed people, may spread beyond exposed skin and is not simply dose-dependent
Photopatch testing, in which duplicate allergen sets are applied and one set irradiated with UVA, is the key confirmatory investigation
Management centres on identifying and withdrawing the responsible agent, rigorous photoprotection and topical corticosteroids for the acute eruption
reference.pathophysiology: Photoallergic contact dermatitis is an acquired, immunologically mediated (type IV, cell-mediated) response. A chemical applied to or reaching the skin absorbs ultraviolet radiation, most often in the UVA range, and is thereby altered to form a photoproduct or a stable hapten-protein complex that becomes antigenic. After an initial sensitisation phase, subsequent exposure to both the chemical and light provokes a T-cell-driven eczematous reaction. Because an immunological memory response is required, only previously sensitised individuals react, the amount of allergen needed is small, and the eruption may extend to covered skin, distinguishing it from the direct, non-immunological tissue damage of a phototoxic reaction.
additionalDifferentials: Phototoxic (photoirritant) dermatitis, which occurs on first exposure and is dose-dependent
Airborne allergic contact dermatitis, which typically involves shaded folds such as the eyelids and submental area
Chronic actinic dermatitis and other idiopathic photodermatoses such as polymorphic light eruption
Seborrhoeic or atopic dermatitis of the face and neck
additionalInvestigations: Photopatch testing with parallel irradiated and non-irradiated allergen series and comparison of the two
Standard patch testing to detect coexisting ordinary contact allergy
Detailed history of topical products, medicaments, fragrances and occupational or recreational light exposure
Phototesting to determine the action spectrum and minimal erythema dose when chronic actinic dermatitis is suspected
Skin biopsy in atypical cases to confirm a spongiotic dermatitis and exclude mimics
Autoimmune serology (e.g. antinuclear and extractable nuclear antigen antibodies) to exclude photosensitive lupus
redFlags: Progression to a persistent, disabling photosensitivity suggestive of evolving chronic actinic dermatitis
Widespread erythroderma or systemic upset raising the possibility of a severe drug reaction
Failure to improve despite allergen avoidance, prompting reassessment for an underlying photodermatosis or connective tissue disease
Features of cutaneous or systemic lupus rather than simple contact photoallergy
reference.prognosis: The outlook is good once the responsible agent is identified and avoided, with resolution of the eczema and no long-term sequelae in most patients; a minority develop persistent light reactivity that may evolve towards chronic actinic dermatitis.
pitfalls: Mistaking photoallergy for simple sunburn or phototoxicity and failing to arrange photopatch testing
Overlooking the sunscreen itself as the allergen, so that increasing photoprotection paradoxically worsens the eruption
Confusing the distribution with airborne contact dermatitis and missing the shaded-site sparing
Attributing a photodistributed eruption solely to a topical agent when a systemic drug is responsible
references: British Association of Dermatologists photopatch testing guidance
management: Identify and permanently avoid the culprit photoallergen, commonly organic sunscreen filters, topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ketoprofen, fragrances or antimicrobials
Institute strict photoprotection with broad-spectrum inorganic UVA-blocking sunscreen, protective clothing and sun avoidance
Treat the eczematous eruption with topical corticosteroids, escalating to a short oral corticosteroid course for severe widespread flares
Confirm the responsible agent with photopatch testing
Relieve symptoms with emollients and antihistamines for pruritus
Monitor for evolution into persistent light reactivity or chronic actinic dermatitis in the minority who do not settle
